Ginette et Gisèle, jumelles et solidaire: Ginette and Gisèle, Twins United in Solidarity

Gisèle, à gauche, et Ginette, à droite,: Gisèle, left, and Ginette, right, are twin sisters who have lived in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood for 42 years. Photo: Pablo Ortiz.
Quartier Saint-Michel, aux abords du bou: Saint-Michel, near Crémazie Boulevard. Along 1<sup>re</sup> Avenue, cars stream past and the city makes itself heard to the rhythm of the still-mild September days. Against the asphalt landscape of the corner, a building that could pass for an elementary school stands out on the horizon. Inside, a string of community organizations firmly rooted in the neighbourhood.
« J’ai une philosophie : “Mon ennemi, c’: “I have a philosophy: ‘My enemy is time. My ally is time,’” Ginette says right off the bat. It is this attitude that lets her not worry too much and keep her feet on the ground and her head held high as she carries out her organization’s mission. Kouzin Kouzin’ supports families and young children in Saint-Michel through its homework help service, its affordable summer day camp and its social and cultural outings.
Ginette Allen, la directrice de l'organi: Ginette Allen, the organization’s director, in the room that welcomes children during activities. Photo: Pablo Ortiz.
Kouzin Kouzin’ a été fondé il y a trois: Kouzin Kouzin’ was founded three decades ago to pair teenagers and children from the Haitian community with mentors. Before long, however, the organization extended its services to everyone in Saint-Michel, regardless of origin. It was a time marked by delinquency and violence, which made headlines and worried families in the neighbourhood. Innovative for its time, Kouzin Kouzin’s approach, built on pairing, helped several cohorts of young people from Saint-Michel stay on course for success. In 2018, Ginette took over from the organization’s founder, determined to carry on her work. Short-staffed, she turned to her sister Gisèle, who needed no persuading to become a volunteer.
Cela fait maintenant six ans que ce duo: For six years now, this nearly inseparable duo, who greet us in almost matching outfits, has held the organization together with sheer effort. Ginette, the pillar of Kouzin Kouzin’, is a versatile woman who looks after everything. Cleaning, helping children with their homework, advising adults in difficulty, writing tedious administrative documents – she does it all. Listening to Ginette, it quickly becomes clear that the organization does a great deal, but that its means to recruit the next generation are limited. “Sometimes Gisèle comes to give me a hand. She came to help me this summer with the day camp when a young 16-year-old employee left me in the lurch halfway through. What do you want me to do with the children? We had no choice; it was Gisèle who was still there, along with one other volunteer,” she explains. Across the table, Gisèle stays quiet but nods, in an unmistakable gesture of complicity with her twin.
Nées à Port-au-Prince, en Haïti, Ginette: Born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Ginette and Gisèle were 18 when they landed in Quebec with their father and their three siblings to join their mother, who was already settled not far from here, on L.-O.-David Street. “We moved in with her right away. We all lived in a 3 1/2. My mother slept on the sofa with my father,” Gisèle recalls.
Le sens de l’entraide, hérité du pays na: The sense of mutual aid inherited from their homeland would make them forget the cramped apartment and the meagre income their mother earned working in a textile factory on Chabanel Street. It was in textiles, on that same street, that Gisèle and Ginette would get their first jobs, two months after they arrived.
Au terme de cette première rencontre ave: After this first encounter with the Quebec working world, Ginette and Gisèle decided to go back to school. In the meantime, they had become mothers themselves. Here again, family mutual aid was crucial. Jeannine, their mother, looked after her grandchildren while the twins studied to become secretaries. “I was beautiful, radiant, I wanted to work at the front desk, welcome people and direct them, (…) I had a funny dream, didn’t I!” Ginette remembers. Gisèle followed the same path with the same fervour.
Toutefois, l’une comme l’autre vont vite: But both quickly became disillusioned after finishing their studies, when they came face to face with racism. “In 1986, I was hired at the Ministry of Education, but it was always for small contracts, y’know, contracts for a Black woman, right,” says Gisèle. Ginette agrees and picks up: “Back then, they didn’t want any little Black folks in the offices; that was the context, and that’s that. They would hire you, but only for three or four weeks, no more. Afterwards, they always found a reason to push you out,” she recalls.
Le temps passe, et l’expérience finit pa: Time passes, and experience ends up building them a thick skin. Known in the neighbourhood for their scrappy side and strong character, the Allen twins are neither timid nor tongue-tied. “Us, we don’t let people walk all over us,” says Gisèle, who says she would be waiting, ready, for anyone who tried to take her by surprise at home. Ginette sings the same tune. “We’re like wasps. You’d better not come into our nest,” she says, eyes full of mischief and her index finger raised.
Quand on lui demande d’où vient leur com: When asked where their fighting spirit comes from, Ginette’s face lights up: “Our great-grandfather, <l1>Richard Allen</l1>, was an African American who freed himself and is famous for his fight for the abolition of slavery. He was the first Black man to found an evangelical Episcopal church for communities of African descent in the United States. He also helped a number of maroons (fugitives seeking freedom, Editor’s note) settle in Haiti. He did a lot for Black rights. Solidarity, the fight, it’s in our family DNA!”
Cet héritage anime Ginette et Gisèle, qu: This legacy drives Ginette and Gisèle, who can’t resist the call to serve the community. The twins adapted and built careers in different fields, from administration to retail, including hospitals and seniors’ centres in Montréal. It is with the strength of these experiences that they keep Kouzin Kouzin’ alive and moving forward today.
L'organisme Kouzin Kouzin' souligne cett: The Kouzin Kouzin’ organization marks its 30th anniversary this year. Photo: Pablo Ortiz.
À tout moment de la journée, Ginette est: At any time of day, Ginette is approached by neighbourhood residents. They know they can always count on her, even when it sometimes goes beyond the organization’s expertise. During our visit to the Kouzin Kouzin’ offices, some residents were there to pick up a letter that was supposed to unblock a family allowance application, others for a document to support their permanent residence applications on humanitarian grounds, or to ask when homework help would resume. “Most of the people who come through here are newcomers, immigrants, among them many single mothers, often precarious workers,” says Kouzin Kouzin’s director.
Membre du conseil d’administration de Ko: A member of Kouzin Kouzin’s board of directors, heart and soul involved in life in Saint-Michel, Alexandre Boucher Bonneau speaks enthusiastically about Ginette, with whom he often talks, and her sister Gisèle. He remembers running into them at the Carrefour populaire, but also at neighbourhood parties, at gatherings at the Maison d’Haïti and during Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day celebrations.
« Il y a beaucoup d’Allen à Saint-Michel: “There are a lot of Allens in Saint-Michel; they’re very present in the community. This family of Haitian origin has been settled in the neighbourhood for nearly 40 or 50 years. They’ve lived here longer than me and my family,” says Alexandre. “Saint-Michel has been struggling for a long time. Many of us are mobilizing, working to improve the situation, but we remain a forgotten, cut-off neighbourhood. Let’s not kid ourselves, Saint-Michel is one of the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods in Montréal and Quebec,” he continues about the neighbourhood where he was born. For him, the immensity of the task must not diminish the importance of the Allen sisters’ persistence in changing things.
D’une certaine façon, l’amour que vouent: In a way, Ginette and Gisèle’s love for their neighbourhood also takes the form of loyalty: they would never leave for anything in the world. “It’s a meaningful place for us, it’s all we’ve ever known. (…) I couldn’t be better off anywhere else, even if others claim otherwise,” says Gisèle. The two sisters take on a grave look before continuing: “Many Haitians have left Saint-Michel. They went to Laval, to Repentigny to buy houses, because they want nothing more to do with Saint-Michel,” says Ginette. “They leave because, often, they have young children, and they know there’s delinquency in Saint-Michel,” begins Gisèle. “Of course there is, but the problem has just been moved elsewhere. So they go to Longueuil, and that’s that,” adds Ginette.
Les soeurs Allen n'entendent pas à rire: The Allen sisters are not joking around when they talk about the problems found in Saint-Michel. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Son visage se durcit quelque peu alors q: Her face hardens somewhat as she continues: “The truth is that Saint-Michel has been covered too much in the media. All the coverage it got kept repeating that it was a bad neighbourhood. I think that’s an exaggeration. Young people were also pointed at a lot, especially young Black people. Yet they’re still just young people hanging out together, right? If it were a group of young white people, nobody would make a big deal of it, nobody would call the police,” says the director, visibly annoyed.
Les jumelles estiment que, malgré son im: The twins believe that, despite its tarnished image, Saint-Michel is nothing like a dangerous place. On the contrary, it is where they can talk with neighbours, take part in neighbourhood life and avoid isolation – another scourge that threatens the most vulnerable people in Saint-Michel.
Si elles conviennent toutes deux que le: While both agree that Saint-Michel’s built heritage has changed a lot over the years, Ginette and Gisèle regret that, with the technological shift, many services are moving online and becoming less accessible, particularly for seniors. “On the digital side, there are services that don’t meet the needs of those who’ve been left behind. Women or men of a certain age, those who are 80, 79, you ask them to go book an appointment online. All health appointments are now made on the computer. [Many seniors] aren’t good with that!” Gisèle points out. A lack of digital literacy, no access to adequate equipment and an Internet connection – the two sisters insist that the neighbourhood is marked by a true digital divide.
Intarissable sur les enjeux complexes qu: Inexhaustible on the complex issues that arise and impose themselves in the neighbourhood, Gisèle softens when she speaks of her fellow residents. “When you go out, when you really meet people, when you take the time to talk to them, they start telling you their problems. You hear them, you listen to them, but sometimes you feel powerless,” she confides.
La liste des griefs qui collent au quart: But the list of grievances attached to the neighbourhood must not hide the good stories that unfold there. “Our own children and plenty of other young people care about the neighbourhood and get involved in it every day. It’s not true that there are only thugs here. Success (...) exists in Saint-Michel too,” says Ginette. She rejects the clichés and explains that what sets her apart from her twin is her pragmatism.
Dans cette génération montante qui se mo: In this rising generation that is mobilizing, Ginette sees the future and the salvation of Saint-Michel. “Today, the neighbourhood is more mixed than ever. At Kouzin Kouzin’, we welcome young Haitians, but also young North Africans, young Latinos, young Sri Lankans. These young people live and grow up together. And that comforts me a lot, it gives me enormous hope.”
La retraite, Ginette n’y pense jamais. E: Ginette never thinks about retirement. She catches herself dreaming of becoming a French teacher at a CEGEP, she who can still rattle off in one breath the fables and plays she learned as a child. Gisèle, for her part, has retired, but still devotes a great deal of time to supporting her sister and Kouzin Kouzin’. “We keep ourselves busy. There’s always something to do, to manage, to sort out. That’s our life, and we love our life,” Gisèle says emphatically.
